subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest, most memorable ending to a persuasive piece?
options: I think I have said enough now.
So yeah, that's about it really.
That is the end of my writing.
The choice is yours: act now, or watch our future slip away.
questions.explain: A direct, balanced final appeal leaves a lasting impression on the reader.

questions.q: In the persuasive acronym DAFOREST, what does the 'F' stand for?
questions.explain: DAFOREST stands for Direct address, Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics, Triplets.

questions.q: A writer shares a short personal story about losing their dog to illustrate a point. This technique is an:
questions.explain: A brief personal story used to support an argument is an anecdote.

questions.q: You are writing a formal letter to your local council. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: So basically the bins are a nightmare.
Bins are well annoying, sort it out.
I am writing to express my concern about waste collection in our area.
Hey, listen up about these bins!
questions.explain: A formal letter requires a clear, polite statement of purpose in Standard English.

questions.q: "It was cruel, heartless and utterly inhumane." The use of three linked words for emphasis is called:
questions.explain: Three items grouped for rhetorical force is tripling (a triplet/rule of three).

questions.q: A newspaper report only quotes critics of a policy and ignores its supporters. This shows:
questions.explain: Presenting one side while leaving out the other is bias.

questions.q: Placing "the richest man in the poorest town" side by side to highlight contrast is:
questions.explain: Positioning contrasting ideas together for effect is juxtaposition.

questions.q: Which sentence best uses 'show, not tell' to convey that a character is nervous?
options: She was very nervous about the exam.
Her hands trembled as she gripped the pencil, her eyes fixed on the clock.
She felt nervous and scared inside.
The girl was nervous because of the test.
questions.explain: Showing physical detail lets the reader infer the emotion rather than stating it outright.

questions.q: Which sentence is a SIMPLE sentence (one main clause)?
options: The dog barked and the cat ran.
Because it rained, we stayed in.
When she arrived, the show began, although it was late.
questions.explain: "The dog barked." has a single main clause, making it a simple sentence.

questions.q: Which of these is a FACT rather than an opinion?
options: This is the best film ever made
The film is too long and dull
questions.explain: A runtime can be checked and verified, making it a fact; the others are judgements.

questions.q: When comparing two non-fiction texts, an exam asks about their "viewpoints and methods." "Methods" mainly means:
options: The techniques each writer uses to put their view across
questions.explain: "Methods" refers to the language and structural techniques used to convey the viewpoint.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the most ambitious, precise vocabulary?
options: The derelict mansion loomed, its decaying facade menacing the street.
The big house was really old and bad.
The old house was scary and big.
The house was very very scary.
questions.explain: 'Derelict', 'loomed', 'decaying' and 'menacing' are precise, ambitious word choices.
